docs.title: fritz_logextractor
docs.text:
Reads the event log of AVM Fritz! devices and writes each new entry once, as a JSON line on stdout, so a log stack (Loki, Elasticsearch, journald, …) can keep it.

The Fritz!Box keeps its event log in RAM: a reboot or a firmware update empties it, and the box has no syslog push. This tool polls the log, works out what is new and prints it. It remembers what it printed, so a restart of the tool or a reboot of the box does not print entries twice.

It talks to the box's TR-064 server only: TR-064 calls give it the uptime, the time zone and the address of the full log (/devicelog.lua with a session ID), which it then fetches from the same server, over HTTP or HTTPS like the TR-064 calls. It does not log in to the web interface.

It is a companion to fritz_exporter, which exports the device's metrics to Prometheus.

Early days

  • Entries are lost if the box logs them and then reboots before the next poll.
  • Checked against few devices: a FRITZ!Box 7690 (FRITZ!OS 8.50) with a FRITZ!Repeater 1200 AX over a day with reboots, and a FRITZ!Box 6660 Cable (FRITZ!OS 8.25) once. Other models and firmware may change their log in ways not handled yet.
  • Remote access to the box is not supported.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
podman run --rm \
  -v fritzlogextractor-state:/var/lib/fritzlogextractor \
  -e FRITZ_HOSTNAME=fritz.box -e FRITZ_USERNAME=logreader -e FRITZ_PASSWORD='...' \
  docker.io/pdreker/fritz_logextractor:latest

{"kind": "event", "event_time": "2026-10-09T08:31:57+02:00", "time_estimated": false, "box_time": "09.10.26 08:31:57", "device": "fritz.box", "host": "fritz.box", "serial": "...", "group": "net", "id": 22, "msg": "Internetverbindung wurde erfolgreich hergestellt. ...", "repeat": 1}
  • Running: locally, in a container, with Compose or on Kubernetes.
  • Configuration: config file or environment, all options.
  • Output: what each field means, repeats, mesh, own logins.

docs.title: Capturing snapshots
docs.text:
To study how a box changes its log over time (folded entries, reboots, timestamps before time sync), --capture DIR also stores what the box sends, next to the normal output:

fritzlogextractor --config config.yaml --capture ./capture > /dev/null

Each device gets a directory below DIR. Every poll adds a line to polls.jsonl with poll time, uptime, model, firmware and the SHA-256 of the log, or with error if the log could not be read (for example while the device reboots). The log itself is stored once per distinct content as <sha256 prefix>.xml, so a log that does not change costs one line per poll.

In the container, use a directory in the volume, for example --capture /var/lib/fritzlogextractor/capture.

Not redacted

The snapshots hold what the box sent: addresses, host and user names and DynDNS tokens. Redact them before you share them.

To see what happens around a reboot, set poll_interval to 10 for the time of the test.

docs.title: Log collectors
docs.text:
Starting points for picking the output up with common log collectors. They are opinionated on purpose; adapt them to your setup. All of them follow the same plan:

  • Sort on kind. Every line the tool writes is JSON: "kind": "event" for the box's log on stdout, "kind": "log" for the tool's own log on stderr. This works even where the two streams arrive mixed.
  • Take the time from the line. Events carry the time the box logged them in event_time, the tool's own lines theirs in time. Without this, a log stack files events under the time they were read, which after a restart can be days later.
  • Few labels or indices. Loki gets the labels kind, device, group (events) and level (own log); Elasticsearch gets one index for events and one for the tool's log. Everything else stays in the JSON.

The files are in examples/ in the repository.

Collector Source Target Checked Grafana Alloy Docker/Podman socket, journald, Kubernetes Loki Docker source end to end with Podman and Loki; all sources with alloy validate Vector Docker Elasticsearch Unit tests with vector test (included) Fluentd Docker fluentd log driver Elasticsearch --dry-run; parsing with sample records Logstash Docker gelf log driver Elasticsearch --config.test_and_exit; filter with sample records

None of the Elasticsearch examples was run against a real Elasticsearch.

Podman

Podman has no fluentd or gelf log driver. With Podman, read the container's log from journald (Podman's default) or through its Docker-compatible socket, as the Alloy and Vector examples do.

docs.title: Grafana Alloy → Loki
docs.text:
Alloy loads every .alloy file of a directory (alloy run /etc/alloy/). Put pipeline.alloy there together with one of the source files, and set the Loki URL in pipeline.alloy.

pipeline.alloy
// fritz_logextractor: sort its lines into the box's events and the tool's own
// log, take each line's time from the line itself and send both to Loki.
// Combine this file with one source-*.alloy; Alloy loads every .alloy file of
// a directory: alloy run /etc/alloy/
loki.process "fritzlogextractor" {
    forward_to = [loki.write.default.receiver]

    stage.json {
        expressions = {
            kind       = "",
            device     = "",
            group      = "",
            level      = "",
            event_time = "",
            time       = "",
        }
    }

    // Few labels on purpose: kind ("event" or "log"), device and group for
    // events, level for the tool's own log. Everything else stays in the line;
    // query it with "| json".
    stage.labels {
        values = {
            kind   = "",
            device = "",
            group  = "",
            level  = "",
        }
    }

    // Events: when the box logged them, not when they were read.
    stage.match {
        selector = "{kind=\"event\"}"

        stage.timestamp {
            source = "event_time"
            format = "RFC3339"
        }
    }

    stage.match {
        selector = "{kind=\"log\"}"

        stage.timestamp {
            source = "time"
            format = "RFC3339"
        }
    }
}

loki.write "default" {
    endpoint {
        url = "http://loki:3100/loki/api/v1/push"
    }
}
Docker or Podman socketjournald (Podman, Quadlets)Kubernetes source-docker.alloy
// The container named "fritzlogextractor", read from Docker or from Podman's
// Docker-compatible socket (mount it at /var/run/docker.sock).
discovery.docker "containers" {
    host = "unix:///var/run/docker.sock"
}

discovery.relabel "fritzlogextractor" {
    targets = discovery.docker.containers.targets

    rule {
        source_labels = ["__meta_docker_container_name"]
        regex         = "/fritzlogextractor"
        action        = "keep"
    }
}

loki.source.docker "fritzlogextractor" {
    host       = "unix:///var/run/docker.sock"
    targets    = discovery.relabel.fritzlogextractor.output
    labels     = {job = "fritzlogextractor"}
    forward_to = [loki.process.fritzlogextractor.receiver]
}

Mount the socket into Alloy's container, for example -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro. With rootless Podman, mount $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/podman/podman.sock there; on hosts with SELinux, also pass --security-opt label=disable.

source-journal.alloy
// The container named "fritzlogextractor" from the systemd journal, where
// Podman writes container logs by default (also for Quadlets). Alloy needs
// read access to /var/log/journal.
loki.relabel "fritzlogextractor" {
    forward_to = []

    rule {
        source_labels = ["__journal_container_name"]
        regex         = "fritzlogextractor"
        action        = "keep"
    }
}

loki.source.journal "fritzlogextractor" {
    path          = "/var/log/journal"
    relabel_rules = loki.relabel.fritzlogextractor.rules
    labels        = {job = "fritzlogextractor"}
    forward_to    = [loki.process.fritzlogextractor.receiver]
}

If Alloy already ships the whole journal, do not add a second loki.source.journal: the lines would arrive twice. Instead, send the lines of the container (__journal_container_name is fritzlogextractor) from your existing source through loki.process.fritzlogextractor.

source-kubernetes.alloy
// Pods labelled app=fritzlogextractor, read through the Kubernetes API.
discovery.kubernetes "pods" {
    role = "pod"
}

discovery.relabel "fritzlogextractor" {
    targets = discovery.kubernetes.pods.targets

    rule {
        source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_pod_label_app"]
        regex         = "fritzlogextractor"
        action        = "keep"
    }

    rule {
        source_labels = ["__meta_kubernetes_namespace"]
        target_label  = "namespace"
    }
}

loki.source.kubernetes "fritzlogextractor" {
    targets    = discovery.relabel.fritzlogextractor.output
    forward_to = [loki.process.fritzlogextractor.receiver]
}

Fits the Kubernetes example (app: fritzlogextractor). Alloy needs RBAC to list pods and read their logs. Only checked with alloy validate.

To query in Grafana:

{job="fritzlogextractor", kind="event"} | json
{job="fritzlogextractor", kind="event", group="net"} | json | id = 22
{job="fritzlogextractor", kind="log", level=~"WARNING|ERROR"}

docs.title: Old entries and Loki
docs.text: On its first start, the tool prints the whole log of the box, which can reach back weeks. Loki rejects lines older than reject_old_samples_max_age (one week by default), so these are lost unless you raise that limit for the first run. Later lines arrive in order, apart from mesh entries a repeater hands over late; those are seconds or minutes behind, well within the hour Loki accepts out of order.

docs.title: Vector → Elasticsearch
docs.text:
vector.yaml
# fritz_logextractor with Vector: sort its lines into the box's events and the
# tool's own log, take each line's time from the line itself and send them to
# two Elasticsearch indices.
sources:
  fritzlogextractor:
    type: docker_logs
    include_containers: [fritzlogextractor]

transforms:
  fritz_parsed:
    type: remap
    inputs: [fritzlogextractor]
    source: |
      parsed, err = parse_json(.message)
      if err != null || !is_object(parsed) {
        abort
      }
      . = object!(parsed)
      # Events: when the box logged them; the tool's own log: when it logged.
      # An event_time without UTC offset (box without time zone) falls back to now.
      stamp = if .kind == "event" { .event_time } else { .time }
      .timestamp = parse_timestamp(string(stamp) ?? "", "%+") ?? now()

  fritz_by_kind:
    type: route
    inputs: [fritz_parsed]
    reroute_unmatched: false
    route:
      event: .kind == "event"
      log: .kind == "log"

sinks:
  fritz_events:
    type: elasticsearch
    inputs: [fritz_by_kind.event]
    endpoints: ["http://elasticsearch:9200"]
    bulk:
      index: "fritz-events-%Y.%m.%d"

  fritz_tool_log:
    type: elasticsearch
    inputs: [fritz_by_kind.log]
    endpoints: ["http://elasticsearch:9200"]
    bulk:
      index: "fritzlogextractor-%Y.%m.%d"

The tests check the parsing and routing without Docker or Elasticsearch; run them after changing the transforms:

vector test vector.yaml vector-tests.yaml
vector-tests.yaml 
# Unit tests for vector.yaml, without Docker or Elasticsearch:
#   vector test vector.yaml vector-tests.yaml
tests:
  - name: an event takes the box's time and goes to the event route
    inputs:
      - insert_at: fritz_parsed
        type: log
        log_fields:
          message: '{"kind": "event", "event_time": "2026-10-09T08:31:57+02:00", "device": "fritz.box", "group": "net", "id": 22, "msg": "Internetverbindung wurde erfolgreich hergestellt.", "repeat": 1}'
    outputs:
      - extract_from: fritz_by_kind.event
        conditions:
          - type: vrl
            source: |
              assert_eq!(.timestamp, t'2026-10-09T06:31:57Z')
              assert_eq!(.id, 22)
              assert!(!exists(.message))

  - name: an own log line takes its time and goes to the log route
    inputs:
      - insert_at: fritz_parsed
        type: log
        log_fields:
          message: '{"time": "2026-10-31T16:30:51.485+00:00", "kind": "log", "level": "WARNING", "logger": "fritzlogextractor.extractor", "msg": "Fritz!Box: could not read the event log (ConnectTimeout), will retry"}'
    outputs:
      - extract_from: fritz_by_kind.log
        conditions:
          - type: vrl
            source: |
              assert_eq!(.timestamp, t'2026-10-31T16:30:51.485Z')
              assert_eq!(.level, "WARNING")

  - name: a line that is not JSON is dropped
    inputs:
      - insert_at: fritz_parsed
        type: log
        log_fields:
          message: "Traceback (most recent call last):"
    no_outputs_from: [fritz_parsed]

docs.title: Fluentd → Elasticsearch
docs.text:
Run the tool's container with Docker's fluentd log driver, tagged fritzlogextractor:

docker run -d --name fritzlogextractor \
  --log-driver fluentd --log-opt fluentd-address=fluentd:24224 --log-opt tag=fritzlogextractor \
  ...
fluent.conf
# fritz_logextractor with Fluentd: Docker's fluentd log driver sends each line,
# Fluentd parses it, takes the box's time for events and writes events and the
# tool's own log to two Elasticsearch indices.
#
# Container: --log-driver fluentd --log-opt fluentd-address=<fluentd>:24224
#            --log-opt tag=fritzlogextractor
# Plugin:    fluent-plugin-elasticsearch

<source>
  @type forward
  port 24224
  bind 0.0.0.0
</source>

# The line arrives in "log". Events take their time from event_time; the tool's
# own log lines keep the time Docker read them, which is when they were logged.
<filter fritzlogextractor>
  @type parser
  key_name log
  reserve_data true
  remove_key_name_field true
  <parse>
    @type json
    time_key event_time
    keep_time_key true
    time_type mixed
    time_format %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z
    # An event_time without UTC offset (box without time zone).
    time_format_fallbacks %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S%z, %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S
  </parse>
</filter>

# One index per kind and day: fritz-event-YYYY.MM.DD, fritz-log-YYYY.MM.DD.
<match fritzlogextractor>
  @type elasticsearch
  host elasticsearch
  port 9200
  index_name fritz-${kind}-%Y.%m.%d
  include_timestamp true
  <buffer tag, time, kind>
    timekey 1d
    flush_interval 10s
  </buffer>
</match>

Needs fluent-plugin-elasticsearch. The tool's own log lines keep the time Docker read them; they are logged as they happen, so that is the time they were written.

docs.title: Logstash → Elasticsearch
docs.text:
Run the tool's container with Docker's gelf log driver:

docker run -d --name fritzlogextractor \
  --log-driver gelf --log-opt gelf-address=udp://logstash:12201 \
  ...
logstash.conf
# fritz_logextractor with Logstash: Docker's gelf log driver sends each line,
# Logstash parses it, takes each line's time from the line itself and writes
# events and the tool's own log to two Elasticsearch indices.
#
# Container: --log-driver gelf --log-opt gelf-address=udp://<logstash>:12201

input {
  gelf {
    port => 12201
  }
}

filter {
  if [container_name] == "fritzlogextractor" {
    # Under "fritz", so the line's fields do not clash with GELF's own
    # (GELF has a numeric "level", the tool's log a named one).
    json {
      source => "message"
      target => "fritz"
      remove_field => ["message"]
    }

    if [fritz][kind] == "event" {
      date {
        match => ["[fritz][event_time]", "ISO8601"]
      }
      mutate {
        add_field => { "[@metadata][index]" => "fritz-events" }
      }
    } else if [fritz][kind] == "log" {
      date {
        match => ["[fritz][time]", "ISO8601"]
      }
      mutate {
        add_field => { "[@metadata][index]" => "fritzlogextractor" }
      }
    }
  }
}

output {
  if [@metadata][index] {
    elasticsearch {
      hosts => ["http://elasticsearch:9200"]
      index => "%{[@metadata][index]}-%{+YYYY.MM.dd}"
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Event times without offset
docs.text: If the box does not tell its time zone, event_time has no UTC offset. The Fluentd and Logstash examples then read it as UTC (or the collector's time zone), Vector takes the time it read the line, and Alloy the time of the line before in the same stream (its default action_on_failure = "fudge"). See Output.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The tool reads its settings from either a YAML file or environment variables, never from both:

  • With --config FILE, only the file counts. All FRITZ_* environment variables are ignored, including FRITZ_POLL_INTERVAL and FRITZ_LOG_LEVEL: set these in the file.
  • Without --config, the environment configures exactly one device.

--log-level on the command line overrides the log level from either source.

docs.title: Config file
docs.text:
The file is the only way to poll several devices. Top-level keys apply to the tool, each entry under devices describes one device:

log_level: INFO
poll_interval: 60              # seconds between polls, at least 10
state_dir: /var/lib/fritzlogextractor

devices:
  - name: Fritz!Box 7690       # shown as "device" in each event; defaults to the hostname
    hostname: fritz.box
    username: logreader
    password_file: /etc/fritz/password
    use_tls: true
  - name: Office box
    hostname: 192.168.123.1
    username: logreader
    password: "..."
    connection_timeout: 0      # no timeout

Only username and one of password or password_file are required per device; every other key falls back to the defaults below. An unknown key, such as a typo, stops the tool with an error that names the closest known key. This also means a config file of fritz_exporter does not work here: give each tool its own file. A file read with password_file may end in a newline; the tool strips it.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
export FRITZ_HOSTNAME=fritz.box FRITZ_USERNAME=logreader FRITZ_PASSWORD_FILE=/run/secrets/fritz
export FRITZ_POLL_INTERVAL=30
fritzlogextractor

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
YAML key Environment variable Default log_level FRITZ_LOG_LEVEL INFO poll_interval FRITZ_POLL_INTERVAL 60 (seconds, at least 10) state_dir FRITZ_STATE_DIR /var/lib/fritzlogextractor devices[].hostname FRITZ_HOSTNAME fritz.box devices[].name FRITZ_NAME the hostname devices[].username FRITZ_USERNAME (required) devices[].password FRITZ_PASSWORD (required unless password_file is set) devices[].password_file FRITZ_PASSWORD_FILE devices[].connection_timeout FRITZ_CONNECTION_TIMEOUT 10 (0 disables it) devices[].use_tls FRITZ_USE_TLS false

state_dir holds one file per device, <hostname>.json. It must survive restarts and be writable; see Running. The file holds message text from the box (addresses, host and user names) and is created readable by its owner only.

use_tls talks to the box over HTTPS. The tool does not check the box's certificate, since Fritz!Boxes come with a self-signed one.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
uv sync --all-groups
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check .
uv run ty check
uv run pytest

Conventions, the design and what the captures of real boxes showed are in AGENTS.md.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs and Material for MkDocs; mike keeps one copy per version on the gh-pages branch.

uv run mkdocs serve            # preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
uv run mkdocs build --strict   # what CI checks on each pull request

GitHub Actions publishes the site:

Trigger Version Workflow push to main dev docs.yaml release (release-please) <major>.<minor>, alias latest release.yaml

The site's root leads to latest, or to dev as long as there is no release.

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
Each new log entry becomes one JSON object on one line of stdout, marked "kind": "event". The tool's own messages go to stderr, also as JSON lines but marked "kind": "log", see Own log lines.

{"kind": "event", "event_time": "2026-10-09T08:31:57+02:00", "time_estimated": false, "box_time": "09.10.26 08:31:57", "device": "fritz.box", "host": "fritz.box", "serial": "...", "group": "net", "id": 22, "msg": "Internetverbindung wurde erfolgreich hergestellt. ...", "repeat": 1}

docs.title: Fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning kind Always event; the tool's own log lines say log event_time When it happened, ISO 8601 with the box's UTC offset (without one if the box does not tell its time zone) time_estimated true for entries the box logged after a reboot, before it had synced its clock; see below box_time The time as the box shows it device, host, serial The device's name from the configuration, its hostname and its serial number group sys, net, wlan, … id The message type; does not depend on the box's language msg The message as the box words it, in its language, without the counter of repeats repeat How many occurrences this line stands for, see Repeats

Every field comes from the box and may hold text typed by someone else, for example a user name in a failed login. JSON encoding escapes it, so it cannot break a line. DynDNS update tokens (q=...) are replaced by q=<redacted>.

docs.title: Repeats
docs.text:
When the same message comes again right away, the box does not add a row: it bumps a counter on the existing row ([3 Meldungen seit …]) and moves the row to the time of the latest occurrence. The tool prints one line per such change, with repeat set to the number of new occurrences and event_time the latest one; the times in between are lost on the box.

A repeat with another message in between gets a row of its own on the box, and a line with repeat: 1 from the tool.

docs.title: Restarts and reboots
docs.text: The tool keeps a state file per device in state_dir, so a restart does not print the log again. A reboot of the box empties its log; the tool notices it from the uptime and prints everything the box logs after it. Entries the box logs in the last moments before a reboot are lost if no poll fetched them.

docs.title: Entries before time sync
docs.text: After a reboot, the box dates its entries 01.01.70 until it has synced its clock, with the time since boot as time of day. Once synced, it rewrites them to the real time. The tool works out the real time from the uptime right away and marks these lines with time_estimated: true. The estimate is within a second or so of what the box shows later. While the box has no time of its own yet, event_time is in UTC.

docs.title: Mesh
docs.text: A FRITZ!Box that is mesh master also shows the log of its repeaters, as rows starting with [fritz.repeater]. Polling the box is enough; polling the repeaters as well gives their entries twice.

docs.title: Own log lines
docs.text:
The tool logs to stderr, by default as one JSON object per line:

{"time": "2026-10-31T16:30:51.485+00:00", "kind": "log", "level": "INFO", "logger": "fritzlogextractor", "msg": "Configured 1 device(s), polling every 60s"}
Field Meaning time When it was logged, in UTC kind Always log level DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR or CRITICAL logger Which part logged it, e.g. fritzlogextractor.extractor, or a library such as urllib3 msg The message exc Only on errors with a traceback: the traceback, in the same line

So a log stack that gets stdout and stderr mixed can still sort events and log lines apart on kind. For reading in a terminal, --log-format text switches to the classic format:

2026-10-31 17:30:51,485     INFO fritzlogextractor | Configured 1 device(s), polling every 60s

docs.title: Own logins
docs.text: Each login of the tool shows up in the log as "Anmeldung einer App" (id 506 or 507), once per session: at start and after connection errors.

docs.title: Running
docs.text: The tool polls each configured device, prints new log entries to stdout and its own messages to stderr. It keeps a state file per device in state_dir, so that a restart does not print the whole log again; give it a place where that file survives.

docs.title: Preparing the box
docs.text:
Create a user on the Fritz!Box for the tool (System → FRITZ!Box Users, German FRITZ!Box-Benutzer), for example logextractor, and give it the right FRITZ!Box settings (FRITZ!Box Einstellungen). Fritz!OS has no finer rights for this; it is the same right fritz_exporter needs.

You may reuse the user of fritz_exporter. A separate one lets you change or revoke either tool's access on its own, and the box's log tells their logins apart.

Use a long random password of at most 32 characters: TR-064 logs in with MD5 digest authentication, and Fritz!OS accepts no longer passwords there.

Mesh

In a mesh, poll the master only: it shows the entries of its repeaters too. Polling a repeater as well gives its entries twice. See Output.

docs.title: Container
docs.text:
Images for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64 are on Docker Hub as pdreker/fritz_logextractor:

Tag Built from develop every push to main <version>, <major>.<minor>, <major>, latest each release, also for linux/arm/v6 and linux/arm/v7

The image runs as nobody (UID and GID 65534) and keeps its state in /var/lib/fritzlogextractor, which is also the default state_dir.

Mount a volume for the state

The image declares /var/lib/fritzlogextractor as a volume. Without -v, Podman and Docker create an anonymous volume, which is gone when the container is created anew, for example on an update of the image. The tool then prints the whole log of the box once more. Always mount a named volume or a host directory there.

docs.title: Podman or Docker
docs.text:
With one device, the environment is enough:

podman run -d --name fritzlogextractor --restart unless-stopped \
  -v fritzlogextractor-state:/var/lib/fritzlogextractor \
  -e FRITZ_HOSTNAME=fritz.box \
  -e FRITZ_USERNAME=logreader \
  -e FRITZ_PASSWORD_FILE=/etc/fritz/password \
  -v ./password:/etc/fritz/password:ro \
  docker.io/pdreker/fritz_logextractor:latest

docker run takes the same options. Arguments after the image name go to the tool, for example --once or --config /etc/fritz/config.yaml (the FRITZ_* variables are then ignored, see Configuration):

podman run -d --name fritzlogextractor --restart unless-stopped \
  -v fritzlogextractor-state:/var/lib/fritzlogextractor \
  -v ./fritz:/etc/fritz:ro \
  docker.io/pdreker/fritz_logextractor:latest --config /etc/fritz/config.yaml

Files mounted into the container must be readable by UID 65534. A named volume takes over the owner of the directory in the image, so it is writable right away. A host directory mounted on /var/lib/fritzlogextractor must be writable by 65534: with rootless Podman, add :U to the mount (-v ./state:/var/lib/fritzlogextractor:U), elsewhere chown 65534:65534 ./state.

docs.title: Compose
docs.text:
services:
  fritzlogextractor:
    image: docker.io/pdreker/fritz_logextractor:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["--config", "/etc/fritz/config.yaml"]
    volumes:
      - ./config.yaml:/etc/fritz/config.yaml:ro
      - state:/var/lib/fritzlogextractor
    secrets:
      - fritz_password

volumes:
  state:

secrets:
  fritz_password:
    file: ./password

with password_file: /run/secrets/fritz_password in config.yaml.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text:
Run a single replica: two copies would each print every entry. Recreate makes sure the old pod is gone before the new one starts, and fsGroup makes the volume writable for UID 65534.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: fritzlogextractor
stringData:
  password: "..."
  config.yaml: |
    devices:
      - hostname: fritz.box
        username: logreader
        password_file: /etc/fritz/password
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: fritzlogextractor-state
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 10Mi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: fritzlogextractor
spec:
  replicas: 1
  strategy:
    type: Recreate
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: fritzlogextractor
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: fritzlogextractor
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsUser: 65534
        runAsGroup: 65534
        fsGroup: 65534
      containers:
        - name: fritzlogextractor
          image: docker.io/pdreker/fritz_logextractor:latest
          args: ["--config", "/etc/fritz/config.yaml"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: config
              mountPath: /etc/fritz
              readOnly: true
            - name: state
              mountPath: /var/lib/fritzlogextractor
      volumes:
        - name: config
          secret:
            secretName: fritzlogextractor
        - name: state
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: fritzlogextractor-state

The state file takes about 150 bytes per row of the box's log: 85 KB for the 567 rows a FRITZ!Box 7690 held after two weeks.

docs.title: Without a container
docs.text:
The tool is not on PyPI. Install it with uv straight from GitHub, or run it from a clone:

uv tool install git+https://github.com/pdreker/fritz_logextractor
fritzlogextractor --config config.yaml

git clone https://github.com/pdreker/fritz_logextractor && cd fritz_logextractor
uv run fritzlogextractor --config config.yaml

The default state_dir, /var/lib/fritzlogextractor, is usually not writable for a normal user. Set state_dir to a directory of your own; otherwise the tool warns, keeps its state in memory only and prints the whole log again on every start.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Meaning --config FILE Read the configuration from FILE instead of the environment --once Read each device once, print what is new and exit --log-level LEVEL Override the log level from the configuration --log-format FORMAT Format of the tool's own log lines on stderr: json (default) or text for reading in a terminal --capture DIR Also store the raw log of each poll, see Capturing snapshots --version Print the version and exit

--once uses the state file as well, so a run from cron prints only what came since the last run.

docs.title: Keeping events and diagnostics apart
docs.text:
Events go to stdout, the tool's own log lines to stderr. Both are JSON lines with a kind field, event or log, so they can be told apart even where the two streams end up mixed, as in a container's log or a terminal. A log stack keeps the lines with "kind": "event" as the box's log and the rest as the tool's own; see Output.

Ready-made configs for Grafana Alloy, Vector, Fluentd and Logstash are in Log collectors.

In a terminal, the classic format is easier to read, and redirecting keeps the events apart:

fritzlogextractor --config config.yaml --log-format text > events.jsonl   # events to a file
fritzlogextractor --config config.yaml --log-format text 2> tool.log      # own log to a file
